step.name: Step 1: Confirm Zoning Eligibility
step.text: Before drawing any lines, make sure your property is eligible for an ADU under local zoning rules. This involves checking with your city's planning department in places like Pasadena, San Marino, or Alhambra, and understanding specific requirements for lot conditions, existing structures, and the type of ADU you envision. They're the authoritative source for property-specific rules.

step.name: Step 2: Prepare Your Documentation Package
step.text: This is where the detailed work happens. You’ll need a comprehensive set of documents including a site plan showing your property boundaries and proposed ADU, detailed floor plans, elevations, structural information, energy documentation, and various required forms. Some jurisdictions might need planning approval before you even submit for a building permit, so gathering everything precisely is key.

step.name: Step 3: Submit for Planning & Building Permits
step.text: Once your documentation is ready, you'll submit it to the relevant city departments. Some cities might allow related trade permits (like electrical or plumbing) to be submitted at the same time as the building permit. California law aims for a relatively quick turnaround, generally requiring approval or denial within 60 days of a complete application. LineWork Development is expert at navigating these submissions, ensuring completeness to avoid delays.

step.name: Step 4: Undergo Inspections
step.text: As construction progresses, various inspections will be required at different stages—foundation, framing, electrical, plumbing, and so on. These inspections ensure that the construction adheres to the approved plans and building codes. Passing these is essential for moving forward with the project and ultimately getting occupancy approval.

step.name: Step 5: Obtain Final Occupancy Approval
step.text: After all inspections are passed and the ADU is complete, you’ll receive the final occupancy approval. This document confirms that your new ADU is safe and ready for use. It's the official green light you need before anyone can move in or use the space. Without it, the unit isn't legally usable.
